claims.text: Trace chromium addition during fabrication will improve the molten-aluminum corrosion resistance of boride-based components.
The improvement will result from formation of a stable chromium-rich alumina surface layer.
Undoped boride-based components are susceptible to molten-aluminum attack under standard hot-dip aluminum-plating conditions.
Typical hot-dip aluminum-plating temperatures are approximately 660–700 °C.
Chromium doping will cause a continuous, thin chromium-rich alumina or Cr-aluminate layer to form on the component surface during high-temperature exposure.
At elevated temperature, chromium dopant migrates to the component surface.
Surface-segregated chromium reacts with oxygen to form a stable protective Cr-aluminate layer.
The proposed Cr-aluminate layer reduces aluminum penetration into the boride-based component.
The proposed barrier mitigates deleterious interfacial reactions relative to an undoped component.
Chromium-doped components will have a lower corrosion rate than undoped boride-based components under identical exposure conditions.
The anticipated corrosion improvement will be observable as lower weight loss and decreased corrosion depth.
Improved performance requires a chromium concentration sufficient to produce a continuous passivating layer.
The chromium concentration must avoid compromising the material's bulk properties.
The chromium intervention may be less effective under overly aggressive flux conditions.
The chromium intervention may be less effective at temperatures outside 660–700 °C.
Preliminary evidence supports a role for chromium in forming a protective layer.
The optimal chromium doping level is not established.
The long-term stability of the protective effect across varied industrial conditions is not established.
